utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. Good afternoon to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-84-T, the Prosecutor versus Ramush Haradinaj et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. This morning a meeting was held between the parties in my presence in which I gave some guidance as far as the objections were concerned in relation to the Rule 92 ter witness statement of the witness to come. We -- I then was not quite certain on some elements where I said that for 80 per cent the Chamber had made up its mind. We have now further considered the matter, and it does not change anything in the guidance I gave this morning to the Chamber [sic]. Then I'd like to turn into private session for a moment.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. The Chamber first gives the reasons for Witness 69 to testify with protective measures. Threats were made against this witness by phone. Further, the testimony of the witness may antagonise persons who reside in Kosovo. The witness -- not a witness but the family of the witness live and work in that territory and have property there. And there exists an unstable security situation in the territory which is particularly unfavourable to witnesses who appear before the Tribunal. So therefore, both under the first standard, that is, threats, and under the second standard, that is, the unstable security situation and a testimony that may antagonise persons - the testimony given by someone who has his family still living there - under both these standards, protective measures are justified. The witness will -- the protective measures granted are pseudonym, face distortion, and voice distortion. Mr. Re, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The summary can be displayed in Sanction, if Sanction is displayable at the moment. There's nothing in it which will reveal the witness's identity.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What follows is the summary of the Rule 92 ter statement of Witness 69. In 1998, the witness worked for the SUP. The Djakovica area of responsibility covered 122 villages in Djakovica and Decane municipality (the Dukagjini area). After the killing of police officer Otovic on the 24th of March, 1998 near Gramocelj, the conflict became more severe. Around April 1998, KLA groups began to emerge in most villages of the Dukagjini area. Intelligence and civilians provided information of KLA headquarters in Glodjane and Jablanica. KLA groups began crossing the Albanian border to collect weapons and equipment - going from Jablanica to Glodjane to Erec, Smonica, Ponosevac, Morina, into Albania. From early spring 1998, the KLA increased its ambushes and attacks on MUP, VJ, and civilian targets and started kidnapping police and civilians, including Serbs, Kosovo Albanians, and Roma civilians and establishing check-points and roadblocks. The KLA became more radical, ambushing cars, buses, and people and opening fire against everything related to Serbia - police, military, and civilians. Serb residents complained of KLA crimes ranging from damage to crops, to rapes, murders and intimidation of people into leaving their homes. The KLA periodically blocked the Djakovica-Decane road, and from 23rd of May, 1998, held it for ten days. It became extremely risky for the police to travel on it and police officers Popadic and Jovanovic were kidnapped there. The area along Lake Radonjic, including Jablanica, Zabelj, Bardonic, and Glodjane, had been a "no-go" area for the police for a couple years and they could only enter if they launched an operation. From mid-1998 to September 1998, it would have been almost impossible to access the area around the lake undetected by the KLA. In late August/beginning of September 1998, there was an operation to unblock the Djakovica-Rakovina-Klina-Pristina road. Around 10 KLA members were arrested in Kodralija and questioned at the Djakovica SUP. KLA members informed the police of the bodies at Lake Radonjic. On 8th of September, 1998, police and DB officials took KLA member Bekim Kalamashi to the Lake Radonjic canal, where he led them to the bodies. The crime scene was then secured 24 hours a day until 19th of September, 1998. Judge Gojkovic's investigation team started work on 11th of September, 1998. Exhuming the bodies and the autopsies lasted until 19th of September, 1998. The witness attended the crime scene on the third or fourth day after the bodies were discovered. The investigation team marked the bodies with numbers, took photographs, and placed them in labeled plastic bags. The police transported remains daily by convoy to the garage of Hotel Pastrik in Djakovica. The remains were constantly secured. The witness attended the autopsies in the basement garage, which was constantly guarded by the police. Identified remains were handed over to relatives and the unidentified remains to the public sanitation company Cabrat. 34 bodies were handed over. On 19th September 1998, 20 body-bags and 1 body-bag with the remains of five individuals were handed over to the Cabrat company for burial at Piskote cemetery. Five more unidentified bodies subsequently recovered were handed over at a later stage. In all, 39 bodies were found at the Canal, Ekonomija farm, and Dasinovac road. That completes the summary of the Rule 92 ter statement of the witness. Witness 69, do you have a copy of your statement there in -- which you signed in Serbian?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber has seen -- I will -- has a copy of it, and I wish to ask you two questions about that document. And the date of interview is the 22nd of May, 2007. My question is: Does it bear your signature and is it true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You're asking me about the statement I provided on the 20th of June, 2007?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That's the one, signed on the 20th of June, 2007.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re, for full position, the cover page of the witness statement says that the interview took place on the 21st and the 22nd of May. I take it that that -- and then we could ignore the cover page Rule 92 ter witness statement where it says "26th of June" handwritten?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So it's the 20th of June. Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The second question is: Would you give the evidence which is contained in that statement if you were asked those questions in court? Would you give the same evidence as is contained in that statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course I would. Those are official data of the police administration in Djakovica, not mine. It is, as is stated here and within some written documents of the police station in Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The statement is 65 ter Exhibit number 1720. On that basis, may it be received into evidence with the redactions which were ordered in the meeting this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Has that already been uploaded in e-court, Mr. Re, or do we still have to wait until we have the final version?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The redacted version has not yet been uploaded into e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So then the Chamber will decide, but if the uploaded version will be the same as this morning, taking into consideration the guidance the Chamber gave in every respect, then the Chamber will decide in favour of admission. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Please turn to paragraph 8 of the statement, Witness 69. In the statement, you referred to a group called the people who want to liberate the villagers who had a base in Jablanica in Djakovica. You say: "The members of this organisation were previously known to the police as criminals who had committed many crimes in those areas. In the beginning the crime they were known to have committed were mainly thefts, serious thefts, fights, and rapes." I want to ask you: What was your understanding of the aim of that group? And in answering the question, I want you to tell the Trial Chamber what the sources were that led you to have an understanding of the aim of the group.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This would be my answer: Much like any other law enforcement agency in the world, we also operate based on our operational connections or links. And I mean the police administration of Djakovica when I say that. We follow operational procedure which encompasses the following: The services in that -- operating in that domain have associates and informants. In terms of operational procedure, such informants and associates have to be registered, provided with a pseudonym and a number, which serves to protect their identity. The information contained herein is the information of the service gained through or by citizens, police officials, operatives, exchanges of information with the State Security Service and the military security service. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Yes. I -- I do understand that. Mr. Re, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You said a moment ago: "there was an exchange of information among the services." Which services are you referring to? And please continue with what you were saying.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I had in mind the State Security Service, since they were very much interested in those issues as well. I also had in mind the military security service and the public security service, which focused mainly on other -- or different issues. However, due to the complexity of the situation, they also assigned us the tasks from that particular domain.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right. What was your -- what I want to find out is what the aim of the group was and how you found out what the aim of this particular group was.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Information that arrived at the police administration as regards the exchange of information with the military security service and the State Security Service and in terms of information provided to my superiors who were in charge, all pointed to the fact that there was something of national interest taking place in the area and that the purpose of establishing such a group was to operate in a way so as to create disorder in the area. As I said, that was State Security Service information that we received. Their end goal was to see Kosovo secede from the Republic of Serbia and to secure a situation within which Kosovo would become independent. That was the information we received from the other two services, since they focused their activities on that. All that information was further corroborated by operational information on certain meetings in certain villages whereby the things I described were discussed. It all pointed at that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Okay. Witness, you then say in paragraph 10: "Around 1995 and 1996, I obtained information from the intelligence of public security and state security that the core of this group consisted of some ten members." What was your information about who the leader of the group was and where did you obtain that information from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I've said already, the services received such operational information from their associates or informants. The informants and associates were not only Serbs or Montenegrins or Muslims but also Albanians and Catholic Albanians. If I remember correctly, during a meeting the State Security Service stated that they had informants and associates who were KLA members. The thing referred to here, that is, the name of Lahi Brahimaj, this is what the operational information was telling us, that he was the head of the group, at least at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And I'm merely conveying --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Could I ask you, please, to look at me a little bit when we're talking so if I need you to pause, I can just put my hand up and down like this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You've answered the question I -- I asked a moment ago. Now, I want you to take you to paragraph 11 of your statement, where you say in the last line, relating to 1998: "The first time I heard of this group which became known as the KLA was a few months before, June 1998, the SUP Djakovica called them by a different name, which was the sabotage terrorist group." What was your information leading up to May 1998 of what the KLA was doing to people within the villages?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, since prior to that time it was defined in the area by a different name, I don't think it's appropriate to ask a question including the name of the KLA because there may be different members of the same or dissimilar groups.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, on the assumption that the 92 ter statement will be in evidence, the witness in 11 explains that the SUP Djakovica called them by -- yes, no, I see we have two -- we have now a third name. Yes, Mr. Re, perhaps it would be good to know for sure that the group called sabotage terrorist group by the SUP Gjakova and the group which became known as the KLA is the same group as the witness was talking about earlier. I think that's the issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was the sabotage terrorist group the KLA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This would be my answer: The official terminology used by the Serbian MUP in the beginning was the terrorist sabotage group. After a while, after we kept coming across emblems and insignia in our operational information, we started using the term "KLA." And therefore that is the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: May I ask you: What do you mean when you say "we were starting to use this term." Who is "we"? Or are there other groups in -- we don't need to go into detail, but maybe we go into private session for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It's -- I think it's generic information available to members of the MUP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: I asked -- actually, I asked the witness and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you asked to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Yes. If maybe that would be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. We'll go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. When you say "we were starting to use this term," Mr. -- Judge Hoepfel would like to know who you refer to. Who's "we"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The official terminology, before the KLA term was used, was the official terminology by the Serbian SUP and the SUP in Djakovica. We used to call them the "sabotage terrorist group" After that we reverted to "the KLA." And when I say "we", I mean the MUP of Serbia and the SUP in Djakovica. I hope I managed to clear that up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we can return into open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Does that answer need to be in private session? Or could it be made public?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, "we" in relation to -- of course, it would identify him as anyone who would be in the SUP or any MUP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It could be public, Mr. Re. Mr. Registrar, that portion of the evidence can be made public. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And, of course, we'll return into open session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you have any information -- oh, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Please proceed, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you have any information, Witness 69, about curfews?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was operational information in circulation within the service stating that once the situation became more complicated that villagers and citizens did not move about after 8.00 p.m. This was corroborated by several reports to the police administration in Djakovica on the events in the field. Some people using roads in that area were stopped, and as far as I recall, some interliners, some buses were stopped and passengers searched.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I was just asking you about curfews, and in paragraph 12 you say: "The KLA imposed curfews after 8.00 p.m." What was your information about the imposition of curfews, as opposed to people not going out after 8.00 p.m.?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The official document was not in the possession of the police administration but on the basis of the movements of the citizens and the operative information official records, it was clear that everything went as I just explained. People were afraid to move about after 8.00 p.m., as I've already indicated to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What I'm trying to clarify is: Your statement says the KLA imposed curfews. There's a difference between the imposition of the curfew and people being afraid to travel after 8.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I -- I've already indicated that as far as I recall, there was no official written document in the possession of the police administration, but on the basis of the official reports, comments about the developments, about what was going on, I tried to explain it the way I just did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I note that the witness appears to be reading from a document. Since the -- his 92 ter statement has gone through a number of changes, it would be helpful to know whether he does need this document and, if so, which one he's using.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. (redacted) I can't see that from here. Are you using any document at this moment? And what is that -- oh, yes. Witness 69. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Apart there the statement that I gave, I don't have any other documents. My briefcase with the information and the documents, it's in -- in my luggage. I didn't bring it here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whenever you would need, Witness 69, to consult the document, would you first ask permission and put it in such a way that you do not read from it. Yes? Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I want to take you to paragraph 17 of your statement in which you refer to the election of Ramush Haradinaj as the commander or KLA commander of the Dukagjini Zone and in which you say that: "The SUP was informed through our intelligence and informants that conflicts were already arising between the KLA and the other so-called liberation army called the FARK." When did you first become aware of the existence of Ramush Haradinaj? And please concentrate just first on when.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that the operational information and the official information about Mr. Ramush Haradinaj dated from 1998, as early as 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And what was the operational information and official information that you had about him before then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, that was in the purview of another service, not the public security. In the course of the exchange of information with that service, as I've already explained when I talked about the time when I heard about the KLA and the elections that had been organised and the appointment of Ramush Haradinaj, that was all in 1998. On the basis of the documents in the possession of the police administration in Djakovica -- or rather, the Decani municipal office for the interior, part of the Djakovica police administration contained information that he is prone to political activity and that on the basis of the criminal record, in the Djakovica SUP it could be ascertained that a member of his family - his father, rather - had been convicted for political reasons. So that was all there was, apart from what the Djakovica police had. So this is the information.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Let's turn to paragraph 19, in which you refer to: "Intelligence, informants, and minutes of KLA meetings", that you became aware of the names of KLA presidents and commanders, and that the commanders of the local KLA branches were suggested by Ramush Haradinaj. What was your information about how the local branches had to operate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, everything that I said in paragraph 19, this is the intelligence gathered by the State Security Service, so the intelligence gathered by the military security service, and the intelligence gathered by the public security service. As far as I can recall, there were some written documents that were found by the service in the field in the course of their activities, daily activities, so written documents about the organisation of the election -- elections in that area for the KLA organs, as indicated here.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was there a KLA programme?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think so. I think so. And I think that the State Security Service did send this document to us. I think that the answer is "yes."

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What was your information about how the KLA branches were financing themselves?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The service had intelligence that they were financed by voluntary contributions, that they were financed from the contributions levied on the salaries or some amounts that were paid on a voluntary basis, something along those lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You just mentioned "voluntary." Did you have any information about involuntary payments to the KLA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, if we consider paying taxes not to the legal state but into some other funds as being involuntary contributions, then the service did have this information.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What if people refused to pay the KLA? Did you have any information on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Information about the refusal to pay indicated that those fellow citizens were subjected to mistreatment, that they were -- well, I don't know what term to use, but quite simply they were pushed to the margins. They were not visited by anyone. They couldn't socialise with anyone. They couldn't go and visit anyone. So it was a form of a boycott.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right. Did it go further than a boycott according to the information you received?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, at one point the service learned that -- that was on the basis of some reports, in the logbook of the Djakovica police administration there were reports that some citizens were abducted, not only Serbs but Serbs, Albanians, Roma, also Roman Catholic Albanians. This information came from the duty service. This is where a citizen would come and report an incident. And the service then was under an obligation to act upon those reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm asking you only at the moment about the consequences of refusing to pay the KLA. Is that what your last answer was referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the basis of the official information, I can say that they were marginalised, boycotted, and there were some reports that some of them had been beaten up. Now, as to what else might have happened, my superiors should know that as well as any services that dealt with this particular aspect.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Let's go to paragraph 22, where it says: "At the same time" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re, just for the record, you're referring to the old paragraphs. And, of course, it will be -- or -- starting "at the same time." I mean, the old paragraph numbering of the -- yes. Because if we ever would come to a point where we admit the new statement, would we then have the same numbers or would it be a tiny little puzzle for whatever Chamber might ...?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The witness didn't sign the chronological revision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: So I've basically abandoned --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The idea of introducing -- so we can forget about any tables of.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Don't forget the table, the table with the ten annexes. Keep that, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the table with the annexes, be I -- but the table -- the paragraph changes table. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Forget that. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right. Paragraph 22 of your statement, Witness 69, where it says: "At the same time, the KLA increased the ambushes and attacks on MUP, VJ, and civilian targets. They also started the kidnappings of civilians and were establishing check-points and roadblocks." How did you see that occurring?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is my answer: This occurred on the basis of the chronology of the events in the field, which was a reflection -- or rather, this is what was reported to the duty service in the Djakovica police administration. Let me clarify this. In our system of work, there is a duty service at the police administration and every citizen can come to that duty service and report about any incidents, anything that happened to him or to his family or anything that he or she may have observed. And on the basis of what the police officers in the duty service received, the official notices, this is what I base my explanation on.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Okay. Did you personally notice any increase in KLA activity in mid-1998?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the basis of the crimes that were reported to the service, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Crimes of what nature? And how did you know that they were KLA-related?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, again, I have to go back to my explanation. These were the reports made by the citizens to the duty service, the crimes that were committed and that were reported by the citizens themselves, so they came in person and said such-and-such thing happened in such-and-such place, and so on. We saw or we observed or we have grounds for suspicion that somebody was done by a KLA member. The reports that were filed by the citizens did not concern only Serbs; they concerned Albanians, Roma, all of the ethnic groups that were present in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Crimes of what nature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, damage to the crops, fights, weapons being discharged, all the way up to the murder of Mr. Otovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Apart from Mr. Otovic's murder, as you described it, what about -- were there other murders or killings ascribed to the KLA in that period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, there were quite a few cases. I can't really enumerate them all off the top of the head -- off the top of my head, but there is paperwork concerning all that. A citizen would report that their house was fired on on such-and-such a day, that such-and-such a thing was done, or that a vehicle was shot at or intercepted. As I indicate, there is paperwork in the Djakovica police administration concerning all that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm obviously in the Trial Chamber's hands in relation to the -- the usefulness of a line of questioning based on generalities of allegations which are, according to Mr. Re's question, ascribed to the KLA during a particular period with there being --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps before we continue this, we are at a time where we would have a break anyhow. So -- Witness 69, we'll have a break of approximately half an hour, but we allow you already to leave the courtroom, where some procedural issue has been raised. But we have to pull the curtains down. Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I think I've taken --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: -- the point as far as it is to be taken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You've taken -- yes. Before we continue, we'll wait just for a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re, this evidence could be considered to some extent cumulative to the extent that this Chamber has heard quite a lot of evidence on what was reported and was linked to the KLA sometimes with, often without greater details. It seems that we have a bit of a -- the same again. What do you intend to do for the remaining time?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Paragraph 24, the last line of paragraph 30, and paragraph 63, and the annexes. Those are the bits which the Trial Chamber ordered redacted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Where the Chamber gave guidance as to -- to redactions. Of course, it was also to some extent because the sourcing was rather unspecific and the allegations were of a rather general nature. So therefore, if you want to elicit that evidence, which, as it is put on paper now is -- well, what we have heard several times before, then, of course, the Chamber would expect you to come with more details about sources, et cetera. Until now you've asked about it, but the answers of the witness were mainly that this is what the services learnt at the time from those who reported this, which is, of course, rather general again. So therefore, to replace one generality by another would not assist greatly. At the same time, I can imagine that if we are talking about, for example, by "control" in the last line of paragraph 30, there it's mainly the witness who should tell us what he understood by that. How much time do you think you would still need for in chief?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I think 20 minutes is probably safe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Twenty minutes is safe.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since you said 20 minutes was safe, we'll strictly limit you, then, to 20 minutes after the break. We'll resume at a quarter past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re. I looked at the clock before I asked you to proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The reason why Judge Orie was looking at the clock, Witness, is because I have 20 minutes to finish with you, so we have to get through these annexes and a few more issues in 20 minutes, so I'd very much ask you to try and keep your answers as brief as possible and as responsive as possible. Okay? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I want to take you to paragraph 24 of your statement in which you say that: "From around early 1998, I had learned from the intelligence and state and public security that the KLA had begun to kidnap people." Did you have any information about detention, KLA detention centres? And if so, what was it? As briefly as possible, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As indicated in my statement, we had intelligence data received from the citizens -- or rather, from people who were apprehended crossing the border illegally or in police raids.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm not -- I'm asking you specifically about detention centres. Did you have any information about the KLA having or not having detention centres? And if so, where were they and what was your information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the service did have operational information that in the village of Jablanica there was a detention unit for the people or citizens who had been abducted. As far as I can recall, there is paperwork concerning all that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Which period are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From mid-1998 until maybe mid-1999, the time period up to the withdrawal.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right. And what about any other places apart from Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Jablanica, the village of Glodjane were mentioned for the most part, and I also think that there were some reports about the village of Rznic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Let's go to paragraph 30 of your statement, in which you refer to the area around Lake Radonjic as being very difficult to reach by car, as there were only dust roads existing. And then you describe the roads into the Lake Radonjic area. What I want to ask you about is KLA control of area -- of areas covered by the Djakovica SUP's area of responsibility. In the period of March through to September 1998, what portion of the area of responsibility of the SUP Djakovica was controlled by the KLA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In that time period, on the basis of the information available to the service, the service could not go to Gornji Ratis, Donji Ratis, Glodjane, Jablanica. It was getting more and more difficult to reach Prilep, the area around Prilep. So that part of the territory down there. As far as I know, even the sector chiefs did not go there to do their daily work. When I say "sector chiefs," I'm talking about uniformed police.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can you give us a rough percentage? Like, 10 per cent? 20 per cent? 30 per cent? Or whatever.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When the situation got more complicated and when all this started, I think that it was impossible to control. It was a large part of the territory, a large percentage of the territory was inaccessible. This was the job of the uniformed police. They were supposed to control that area. And on the basis of the exchange of information, large areas were inaccessible to the police to carry out their basic daily work.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Let's go to paragraph 63 of your statement. In the preceding paragraph, 62, you refer to police documentation being destroyed during the NATO bombing in 1999 and the SUP Djakovica building being completely destroyed. And then you referred to photo records and fingerprints of the KLA terrorists arrested in September 1998 possibly being destroyed as well. Do you remember seeing information on Idriz Balaj, also known as Toger? Firstly, yes or no. If the answer is "yes," I'll ask you another question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the question. I didn't hear it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Have a look at paragraph 62 of your statement, please. Did you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right. Can you please have a look at paragraph 62. It's in front of you there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I've had a look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right. My question is: In paragraph 62, you say that you think or possibly some records relating to KLA terrorists arrested in September 1998 were destroyed in a NATO bombing. My question was: Did you have any information about -- or did you remember seeing any information about Idriz Balaj, also known as Toger?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was some operational information. These records were destroyed in the NATO air campaign. And this third part about the fingerprints, I'm not sure that his fingerprints were there. And as far as other members are concerned, the sum of whom had been apprehended in police raids, I'm sure that their fingerprints were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Okay. Please concentrate on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness 69.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: -- the questions I'm asking you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness 69, Mr. Re asks you whether among that material, that information, documentation that was destroyed by the NATO bombing, whether you have any recollection or whether there was any material in it which related to Idriz Balaj, also known by the name of Toger. That's the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I want to show you some documents. Can the witness please be shown -- be given a bundle of documents here, which are the annexes referred to in his statement. Do you have the -- there's a bundle of documents there. The first one I want to take you to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, before we -- we have bundles with different numberings. Mr. Re, for us to follow, should we focus on the list of ten? Annex index? Yes? Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The first one I take you to is annex 1, which is a map of the area of responsibility of the Djakovica SUP, which is 65 ter number 1722 and it is referred to in your statement as annex B.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It needs a number, Mr. Re?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It needs a number?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be marked for identification as P1175.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The question is simply: Is that a map -- is that a map of the area of responsibility of the Djakovica SUP; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you. The next one is number -- annex 2, which is 65 ter Exhibit number 1723, which is a list of villages within the area of responsibility of the Djakovica SUP. And it is referred to in the statement as MSBK 3. Can the witness please have a look at that and confirm that is in fact a list of villages so described.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, that would be number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be marked for identification as P1176.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The next one I refer you to is a Djakovica SUP report number 307/98 on Rade Popadic's kidnapping. That's annexed as number 3, 65 ter number 1725, which is referred to in your statement as MSBK 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, that would be number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that would be number P1177.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Is that the document as described in your statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The next one I take you to is described as annex 4, which is MS -- sorry, 65 ter number 1726, described in your statement as MSBK 5, which is a report number Ki1 or 17/2005, relating to the handover of exhumed remains by UN representatives. Is that the document in question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, may I take it that that receives number 1178? Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The next one, annex 5, 65 ter number 1727, described as a map showing the no-go area for the police between mid-1998 and September 1998, which is described in your statement as annex A. Is that in fact the map you marked as the no-go area, which is annexed to your statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would prefer to wait until it appears on my screen so that I know what we are talking about, but already, Mr. Registrar, may I take it that that would be marked for identification as 1179? Thank you, Mr. Registrar, for the confirmation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The 65 ter number on that last one --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Maps usually take a bit more time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It actually has his signature on it, so I'd ask that it not be displayed publicly, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, not to be displayed in public. And marked for identification under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm informed that everything is only displayed in the courtroom. But still my screen is empty for the last one; that's 1179.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re, could you please repeat the 65 ter number for the map marked with the no-go area so -- because it seems that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness 69, is that the map with the no-go area marked on it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The next one is annex 7, which is 65 ter number 1728, described as Djakovica SUP criminal investigation -- "Criminal report on the crime scene investigation of Lake Radonjic," which is described in the witness's statement as "annexed document." Please look at that document and confirm that that is as described. Oh, did I miss annex 6 just then? I apologise. Can I -- I take you back, Witness, to the previous document, which is annex 6, 65 ter number 1729, described as "SUP report on the arrival at the location in Lake Radonjic," and it's described in your statement as annex 1. Is that the document in question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Registrar, may I take it that that would receive number P1180 for marked for identification? Yes. Thank you for the confirmation. Please proceed, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Okay. Next one, number 7, I referred you to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd like to see it, but perhaps I'm -- yes, that is the -- the original is on the screen. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right. The next one was annex number 7, 65 ter number 1728, described as "Annex to document" in your statement. The description is "Djakovica SUP criminal report on the crime scene investigation." Is that the document in question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, would that receive P1181, marked for identification? Thank you for the confirmation. Please proceed, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The next one is annex 8, 65 ter number 1730, described in your statement as "Annex 2, KLA journal excerpt for beginning of May 1998." Is that the document in question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, would that receive P1182, marked for identification? Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Please proceed, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The next one is described as annex 9, 65 ter 1731, described in your statement as "Annex 3," described as "SUP Djakovica official note from citizen, (redacted) Is that the document in question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, would that receive number P1183, marked for identification? Thank you for confirming that. Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The last document is annex 10, 65 ter 1732, which is described in your statement as annex 4 and it is case file compilation of documents dealing with formation of the KLA in Metohija. Can you please look at that document and confirm that is the document in question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. If I might, just for purposes of -- of clarity, with regard to annex number 10, if I could ask for the ERN numbers for -- just for that particular annex for the moment, I'd appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, I'll first -- yes, I wanted to check on the transcript whether this speed could be followed. And I'd like to express my admiration that the transcriber was able to follow this. That is now on the screen. Could you put the question or repeat the question to the witness, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Is that the document in question annexed to your statement? I think it's in the other volume of documents which are to your left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, could you please assist the witness. Meanwhile, Mr. Registrar, would that receive P1184, marked for identification? Mr. Registrar, you're nodding. Thank you for your confirmation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you. And there is one last question I want to ask you, and that relates to KLA communiques. Firstly, I want you to answer "yes" or "no." Did you see any KLA communiques in 1998? Just "yes" or "no."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did they -- how did they relate to things which you had witnessed or read about yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question. I didn't understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How did the KLA communiques that you read in 1998 relate to things that you had seen or read about or heard about yourself in your area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I truly cannot understand. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness 69, what Mr. Re would like to know from you is whether what you read in the communiques, whether that was in line with or not in line with your own findings or what was reported from other sources to you. So was it congruent or was it different what you read there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was in keeping with what we found out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, by your own means you mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. By police work, if that's what you mean. By our operative work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Any further questions, Mr. Re? Witness 69, you'll now be cross-examined by Defence counsel. Mr. Emmerson will be the first one to cross-examine you, and he's counsel, as I said before, for Mr. Haradinaj. Mr. Emmerson, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And, Your Honours, may I indicate straight away, out of the interests of efficiency, given that much of this witness's testimony in the 92 ter statement traverses ground that has been covered in the statements of other witnesses and about which there has been some fairly extensive cross-examination by reference to documentary sources, I do not propose to repeat the exercise with this witness of putting to him material that has already been put to and explored with other witnesses involved at various stages, and so I propose therefore to take my cross-examination of this witness rather more shortly than I would do, for example, with some of the early witnesses, if Your Honours are happy with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson, may I take it that this, perhaps among other reasons, also for the reason that direct knowledge of some of the documentary evidence seems not to be within the -- within the reach of this witness where he did not take any statements or where he -- so to ask him to comment on statements taken by others where we have already a more direct -- a more direct evidence on --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. And I -- I trust that the approach I take will tread a path between generality and detail which -- which is acceptable to the Trial Chamber. In other words, I don't propose to put other detail that has already been put in the past.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And the Chamber considers all the evidence in the context of the totality of the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Before Mr. Emmerson starts, can I just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: -- ask for a redaction of one line at page 50, line 5. There are two words in that line which perhaps should be redacted for abundant caution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're referring to a name? Yes. Mr. Registrar, would you please prepare the redaction. Mr. Emmerson, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Witness 69, can I please ask you to turn to paragraph 31 and 32 in the statement that you have signed. And whilst that's being done, might I ask, please, Mr. Registrar to pull up Exhibit P1152. Witness 69, you -- focus, please, if you will, on the first few lines of paragraph 31 for a moment where you say this: "The area around Lake Radonjic had been a no-go area for the police for a couple of years. This included the villages of Jablanica, Zabelj, Bardonic, and Glodjane. This meant that it was rare for police controls to go into this area and it was only possible if the area was secured." Now, I just want to explore, please, with you in a couple of questions what you mean by that. Could you perhaps look on the screen. The document that you're there looking at and I'm concerned with the first bullet point that appears there, and a report by Colonel Bozidar Delic of the 549th Motorised Brigade dated the 23rd of March, 1998. And if you can just get a sense, please. We note that there may be a translation error in respect of the words in the first part of the paragraph, paragraph 1, but if you look at the first bullet point, it reads that: "On the 22nd of March, around 3.00, belts of 7.62-calibre bullets and various other items" - I'll just summarise - "were found in several places in the area of the village of Donji Bites in the forest towards Radonjic Lake. The Djakovica MUP organised an ambush in that area on the 22nd/23rd of March, 1998 but no one showed up, by the morning hours." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: We can infer from that, can we, that officers from the Djakovica MUP were, from time to time, at least, conducting operations in that area in March of 1998?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Based on the document, one would say so. However, as regards this issue, there are some other officers there. I cannot give you an exact answer as to whether there were or there were none. It wasn't done by us. It was done by the uniformed police of the police administration in Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Nonetheless, the words in paragraph 31 where you speak of police patrols not entering this area for a couple of years, I mean, do we understand those to be uniformed police patrols that you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Just help us, please, because it -- you -- I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: You indicate that it was rare for patrols to go into the area and it was only possible if the area was secured. Can you just give us a sense, please, of the frequency of it from -- from March onwards.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: According to the reports presented at the collegium meetings within the police administration in Djakovica, the superiors of the uniformed part of the police stated that the uniformed police is unable to conduct patrols and enter the wider area referred to in order to try and establish and preserve public peace and security. Let me try and clarify that. The reports referred to were the reports of the uniformed part of the police. They were the most credible source of this information and the best information can be provided by their officers and superiors. I am not trying to avoid answering your question; however, I cannot claim something that I'm not 100 per cent sure of.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Well, that's all I want to be clear about. You -- is it the position now that you're not 100 per cent sure one way or the other how often the uniformed police patrolled in that area? Is that the position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Precisely so.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Again, if we can return, please, to paragraphs 31 and 32 in your statement. You there refer to -- or, I'm sorry, you there assert that the Serbian police stopped going into the area on police patrol during the second half of 1998 altogether unless they launched a police operation? And then in paragraph 32, you refer to the map, which is annex 5, showing what is described as the no-go area, which you describe as the area where the police could not enter from mid-1998 until September 1998." Do you -- do you have the passage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Again, I'm simply trying to understand at the moment what those assertions amount to, because it -- you appear to be suggesting that once mid-1998 was reached, although there were operations conducted, they were less frequent than they had been in the first half of the year. Is that a correct reading of your statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I fail to understand the question. However, if you're asking me to explain paragraphs 31 and 32, things were as described here. It is based on the reports of superiors from the uniformed part of the police in Djakovica. Those superiors were in charge of securing public peace and order. They stated that their employees could not enter the area in order to do that. I was not one of the superiors in that department; therefore, I can only convey to you what was mentioned at collegium meetings of the police administration in Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Forgive me, because I'm simply at this stage trying to understand exactly what it is that you yourself are saying in these two paragraphs about the information that you had received. And you -- you appear to be saying in paragraph 31 that the Serbian police stopped going into the area on police patrol during the second half of 1998, which on one view would imply that they were entering on police patrol during the first half of 1998. Is that correctly understood or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Perhaps the police did go there during that period but seldom. Again, I have to say that you should ask this of those in charge of the uniformed police. I merely repeated what they had said at collegium meetings of the police administration in Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Very well. And -- and just focusing then on what they had said to you about the second half of 1998. Again, is it -- is it correctly understood that your testimony is that you were told that they did not enter the area marked on your map as annex 5 until September 1998? Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know how to give you the most precise answer possible. What it says here in paragraphs 31 and 32 is based on the statements made by the police officers in the uniformed police. It is possible that the uniformed police did go there regularly. It's possible. I cannot either confirm or deny that. But you could get the most adequate answer from the police officers -- commanding officers who made their reports at the morning briefings at the police administration in Djakovica, so that my answer is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness 69, you gave a statement. You have now explained to us several times that -- at least in this respect, that your statement was based upon what you heard. If Mr. Emmerson seeks further details of what you may have heard -- you either remember those details; then you could tell Mr. Emmerson. Or you don't remember any further details; and then you have to say, "I don't remember." But there's no reason for you to say, "Ask someone else." I mean, you gave the statement and we are seeking to understand the statement to the best of our abilities. What now Mr. Emmerson would like to know is the following: That where in paragraph 31 you state that only under very special circumstances, that is, only if the area was secured, the police would go in there; that you at the same time say that the Serbian police stopped going into the area on police patrol during the second half, so that it was different. Now, the question specifically put to you by Mr. Emmerson is whether during this second half of the year 1998 until early September, whether you heard during the meetings of the police going into that area at all. That's what Mr. Emmerson would like to know. At least, Mr. Emmerson, if I ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Mr. President, I did not want to indicate that you should call somebody else to testify. I testified to the best of my knowledge everything that I knew, everything that I could recall. I don't know how I could provide you any other information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question is quite simple: On from mid-1998 until September did you learn during your meetings with the colleagues, as you described before, did you learn of the police patrols entering into that area at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Proceed, Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And can you tell us again, please, with what frequency they were entering into that area during the second half of the year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. And were -- were you aware of the involvement of police units in a major offensive with the VJ between the 9th and the 11th of August, 1998?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Are you distinguishing, for the purposes of your answers, between police units and units of the PJP or are you including the PJP within your definition of "police units"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the PJP and the police force, the police forces. All the elements that wore uniforms, that were not plain clothes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Now, as for the uniformed police, I may recall something about actions that were carried out in concert, but plans, march routes, the strength, the activities, this is definitely not in my purview.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: It may be the way I asked you the question, but line 60 [sic], my question was: Were you aware of the involvement of police units in a major offensive with the VJ between the 9th and the 11th of August? Now, can you answer the question if I put it slightly differently? Did you know that MUP or PJP units had participated in an offensive directed, for example, at Gllogjan between the 9th and the 11th of August?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The gestures of the witness seems to indicate that he doesn't know. Do you know or don't you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't remember. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Could we look, please, at Exhibit P1181, which is annex 7 to your witness statement. Do you have that available to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I only have my statement. Nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Okay. I think -- perhaps --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you look at the screen, it will appear for you on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, I'm sorry because of the changes in exhibit numbers that this may not be as smooth as would normally be the case, but what I'm seeking is, so far as the English translation is concerned, if we could pick it up on the page numbered 9 -- I'm sorry, 8 at the bottom; and so far as the B/C/S version is concerned - just bear with me one moment - it will be the page with 7573 in the top right-hand corner. It should be -- KU196 is the first reference. I'm sorry the pagination has changed from one exhibit to another. This is a document that was annex 10 to the 92 ter statement of Mr. Radovan Zlatkovic but is also produced by this witness. And there is a record in the document of a series of armed engagements taking place all under the reference "KU." It might -- it might really assist the witness to take it, I think, in the hard copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And, I'm sorry, could I ask Mr. Registrar to take it to the page before. That -- the one we have up on the screen, I think, is page 9. It's certainly page 9 on my pagination. If we could just start on page 8. And, Madam Usher, the ERN number in the top right-hand corner should be 7573. Can I -- perhaps -- it might be the -- the easiest and simplest and most practical way might be to hand the bundle to me and I'll find the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson, you're invited to give e-court page numbers for the registrar, because it's far easier for him to -- to find it that way and so we lose --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: The difficulty we have is because these exhibits were organised in a different fashion from the first to the second 92 ter statement and then we had the difficulties that we had this morning, it's simply not possible to do it in that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: But I think the witness now has the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can you see, Witness 69, that you -- you're looking at a series of entries, each of them with the initial "KU" and then a number and then the year 1998? Do you have that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And for the English translation -- yes. We're -- we're also looking at page 8 of the English translation. I think at the moment we have page 3 on the screen. So it should be "68" in the top right-hand corner. I just want to take this rather more briefly than so far it's gone. But if you look at the first entry about a third of the way down that page, KU 196/98, it records that on the 9th of August, 1998, at about 7.30 hours in Biteska Suka sector, Gjakova municipality, an ethnic Albanian DTG carried out a terrorist attack firing at members of the Serbian MUP. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be asked to speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please come closer to the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, obviously that's right within the area you've marked on annex 5. You would agree with that, would you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And if I can take it very shortly - and I'll be corrected if I put anything to you wrongly. I don't want to go through each and every entry. But in this document that's exhibited to your statement, there are eight entries under the references KU 196, 205, 217, 218, 220, 222, 406, and 430, each of which involves an armed engagement between the 9th and the 11th of August in the area within your marked section in annex 5, Suka Bites, Bites village, Dujak, Gramocelj, and in the area of Gllogjan. Now, presumably, Witness 69, you would have been aware of those incidents, wouldn't you, reported as terrorist alleged crimes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And in each instance they're recorded as having involved armed attacks on the MUP carrying out regular assignments and duties. Can you help at all, please, to explain in the language of the records that you're familiar with what that expression is intended to convey, "regular assignments and duties"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, again we're dealing with the uniformed police of the Djakovica police administration. The regular tasks and assignments -- and assignments or activities would comprise sector activities and securing that area and also patrol duties, ensuring the free movement of citizens and goods. That's as far as I am able to understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: If that -- if that were right, Witness 69, that would imply, wouldn't it, that during this period of August the uniformed police were involved in regular patrols in that area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the basis of what it says here, it is so -- or rather, that they attempted to re-establish law and order in these areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: All right. To move to another topic briefly. Could we turn to annex 10 to your signed witness statement, which is now ...

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: It's 65 ter 1732, and it's a fairly lengthy document. If -- if the references have transferred correctly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is now marked for identification P1184. Is that the one?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That's the one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. If the references have transferred correctly, it should be pages 26 to 30 in the English translation and pages 21 to 24 in the B/C/S. The B/C/S is certainly correct. In fact, if we can take it to the bottom half of the page in B/C/S, that would be helpful. And in the English, pages 26 to 30. Yes, and, again, if we can focus in on paragraph 1 at the bottom of the page. You presumably read these documents in the preparation of your statement, Witness 69; is that right? If you'd just bear with me and focus on the question for a moment, if you would. You considered these documents before you came to sign your witness statement; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Are you referring to my statement? Yes, I did read and I did sign it.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: You've produced these documents as annexes to your statement, Witness 69, and so the question I'm asking you is whether you read them before you annexed them to your witness statement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I assume that I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Without going through all of the following pages, this document refers to alleged KLA attacks perpetrated by the KLA from the village of Baballoq. And, again, in -- in summary, over the pages which follow, it lists a total of 14 alleged incidents dating from the 2nd of May to the 27th of July directed either at MUP check-points in the area of the Baballoq refugee camp or at MUP members positioned at Erecka Suka or at MUP positioned within the refugee camp or, in one instance only - and I think this is item number 11 - at a VJ army helicopter. Now, the questions I want to ask you about this document are these: We have heard some evidence from a PJP commander called Rade Repic who had responsibility for Baballoq during May and June. First of all, is that a gentleman whose name you recall at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, barely, but more yes than no.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: He is -- he has testified that PJP officers would be located physically within the houses of the Baballoq settlement closest to the road and would occupy those premises. Is that something that you were aware of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can you tell us, please, from your own recollection - it may be that your memory doesn't assist you sufficiently - but can you tell us as to when the MUP or PJP first began securing the area around the Baballoq refugee settlement with check-points and by stationing forces at Erecka Suka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'll move to another topic. You describe in your statement at paragraphs 33 to 34 the arrests and interrogations of a group of men from Kodralija. Do you have a recollection now of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the statements, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can you remember those men being brought into the police station, Witness 69?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Were any of them in their underwear when they were brought in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know that with any certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Well, did you see them being brought in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't remember the exact moment when they were brought in, but I remember the time when they were brought in for an interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nebojsa Avramovic has testified in relation to their processing as Gjakova police station when they were brought in by officers of the PJP and has testified that he believes that at least some of them were brought in in their underclothes. Do you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson, could you give us the --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. That's 6626, lines 11 to 13.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Is that something you would expect to have been informed of, Witness 69, if suspects had been brought in in their underclothes after arrest?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's possible that they were brought in, but I really can't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber has -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But nobody reported that to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber has seen and heard the contents of a statement made by Bekim Kalamashi, which was marked as D142 and was read into the transcript between pages 6627 and 6630, as well as other statements from the men arrested at the time, in which it is alleged that prior to being brought into the police station they were beaten by PJP officers and that after being brought into the police station, they were systematically beaten whilst in custody.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What's the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: The question is: Do you have any comment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as the PJP members are concerned, I don't know that. That's for sure. And as for people being beaten up once they were handed over to the OKP service, I don't know anything about that, but I'm almost certain in saying that this was not so.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Did you often during this period receive allegations of police officers ill-treating people in custody?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was not within my purview, anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So you -- you don't recall any incidents in which people were complaining that they have confessions or statements beaten out of them at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There may have been things like that, but I'm sure that there were no such instances in the service where I worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And whose responsibility would it have been to investigate the involvement of police officers in that sort of activity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The police control service and the police sector, the uniformed police. They were dealing with the legality of the policework in any given police administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And -- and do you have any recollection of that unit conducting any inquiries in your police station in 1998 or 1999, Witness 69?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Could I ask you, please, now on another topic to turn to paragraph 35 of your statement. I'm sorry, paragraph 36 of the old statement. Could we please bring up D171. Witness 69, your record and recollection is that amongst those who first attended the canal were General Colonel Vlastimir Djordjevic and Lieutenant General Obrad Stevanovic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And I think at annex 6 to your witness statement you have produced a record signed - bear with me just one moment - I'll come back to that topic. You have, I think, in your documentation a record to that effect; is that correct? You recall seeing that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can you help us at all as to how it came about that two such high-ranking officials took part in what was basically a search operation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just for the record, we are now talking about P1180, Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I don't know whether you heard my question, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember it, and this would be my answer: Based on the information on the events there, and on orders of the then-head of police administration - and I suppose he did that in agreement with his superiors - those people that I mentioned in my statement attended the crime scene. I was ordered by the head of police administration to remain in the building; therefore, Generals Djordjevic and Stevanovic attended this scene. From the police administration, there was Adamovic and I don't know who else.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Perhaps I should put the question from a slightly different standpoint. Would it have been usual for somebody of General Colonel Djordjevic's seniority to attend a search operation of this kind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The knowledge of that taking place was of great importance. I suppose because of that they all participated and went to the crime scene. That is my thinking, my view of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I wonder if we might just go into private session for one moment, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Please proceed, Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Witness 69, in paragraph 31 of your statement you state that "It was only possible to go into areas such as Jablanica if the area was secured." By "secured," do you mean by the VJ? And if not, by whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First of all, good evening, Mr. Harvey. And the answer to your question is that the area was secured by the police or by military forces.
