utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Would you agree that there was very close cooperation between the police and the military on the occasions when any attempt was made to penetrate Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Were you involved in those plans yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: You mentioned at page 34, line 22 today, you talked about written documents that were found by the service in the field. May I take it that one of the objects of your researches was to discover as many documents as you could that appeared to be written by members of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was one of our tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Were you aware of such documents being seized in the village of Jablanica? At any time during 1998.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think so, and I believe the State Security Service later became involved in the matter of those documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Was that the means by which your service came into possession of minutes of meetings held by members of the KLA in that area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let us suppose so.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Was it also one of the instructions given to your service in the field to destroy the headquarters or houses of KLA members?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you please repeat that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Was it also one of the instructions given to your service in the field to destroy the headquarters or houses of KLA members?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly not.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: You are aware, I presume, that the police forces entered Jabllanice on the 2nd and 3rd of August, 1998, are you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Well, does that mean perhaps you're aware or perhaps that was the date or perhaps you remember? Could you explain your answer, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The latter. I cannot remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Well, is it that you remember that they did enter Jablanica at sometime; you just don't remember the exact date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't recall the date at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: But you do recall that they entered Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some people said so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness 69, you increasingly start by not answering questions and say "let's suppose so, could be." Please answer the questions. The question was whether you recalled that they entered Jablanica, whether you were told that this happened. Then Mr. Harvey might want to know who told you. But please focus on the questions and answer them. Please proceed, Mr. Harvey. So the last question was whether you recall that they entered Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Mr. President, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: You've no idea if they ever entered Jablanica at any time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know how to make it clear to you. Yes, they did, but I don't know the time or the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know how else to put it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's fine. But that's -- your previous answers were not fully corresponding with -- to what you tell us now. So you knew that they were entering Jablanica but you don't remember the date. Please proceed, Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: One of your responsibilities would be to investigate whether any crimes had been committed at Jablanica; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: You have told this Trial Chamber that you had information that there was a prison at Jablanica. What investigations did you have carried out into the truth or otherwise of there being a prison in Jablanica when your forces, the Serb police, were in Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Apart from official notes and the operative material that existed, the members of that team never investigated on the spot in Jablanica where it was rumoured there existed a prison or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: They never looked to see if they could find bodies of people who had allegedly been abducted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My answer is "no."

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: They never looked to see if they could find evidence of beatings or torture?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have to say "no" again.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: In fact, you never received a report from any of your men in the field who had entered Jablanica that they had ever found anything that they could call a prison there, did you?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: In -- in what time period are we referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: In 1998. Let us say the two occasions in 1998. And I will be specific about dates. The beginning of August and the beginning of September 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Is that clear enough for you, Witness 69?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So is it correct therefore that you never received from any of your men in the field who entered Jablanica in August or September of 1998 any report that they had found anything that they could call a prison there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: At this point, Your Honours, I think it's going to be necessary for us to go into private session. I have some specific questions to put to the witness about his own responsibility for matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I am sure that you would agree, would you not, sir, that the following list would constitute forms of ill-treatment if they were used: The use of rubber batons, kicking, rifle butts, pistol butts, metal bats, baseball bats, electric shock, and finally, the use of fists or hand slaps when discussing anything with a potential - for purposes of our discussion - witness? Those would be forms of ill-treatment, would they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Would it be appropriate, in -- in your opinion as a police officer, when interrogating an individual to use any of the forms of physical behaviour that I have just mentioned as a method of obtaining information from them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All of the things -- or rather, not all of the things you mentioned strike me as logical; however, on occasion some policemen may have used force but only out of those which are deemed acceptable or are allowed.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And with regard to those kinds of force which are deemed acceptable or allowed, would the punching of a woman in the face be an acceptable form of physical use when speaking to her about a matter of serious import?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, could you come to your point, because until now these matters are all rather obvious.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Are you aware of allegations -- And if we could have P6, which is the Spotlight Report, and I believe that it's page 31, up on the screen. And I don't know whether or not there is a B/C/S translation. I believe that there's not. So I'm -- I'm going to read something to you, sir, and ask you to comment on it. And this is with regard to an investigation that was occurring. "Besa Arlati, member of the Democratic Alliance of Kosovo organisation in Djakovica was questioned at the Djakovica police department several times in connection with abductions of officers Popadic and Jovanovic. The first time was on 26 May when police chief Sreten Camovic demanded that she tell them everything she knew about the alleged abduction. Besa Arlati said the police inspectors cursed her 'Albanian mother' and called her a whore and Chief Camovic punched her in the face. She was held all night in a cellar flooded with sewage some 10 to 15 metres deep."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Centimetres.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Oh, thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: "On 28 May, she was questioned continuously for nine hours." I pause. Were you aware of those allegations being made against Sreten Camovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Were such a thing to happen, would that be appropriate police behaviour? And I believe you told us that the punching in the face would not but the placing of a person in sewage water overnight, would that be appropriate police investigative technique?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Absolutely no.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Do you know of any investigation being done at the Djakovica police department by anyone concerning these allegations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just for our information, Mr. Guy-Smith, I have some difficulties in finding this on page 31 of the ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: It's the right bottom quarter -- corner, and it's under 2.24.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Did you find it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Good.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, thank you. Mr. Re, is there any need to re-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: No, no need for re-examination. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber also has no questions for you at this moment, Witness 69. The only thing that then remains is to look at the annexes to the statement, that is, P1175 up to and including P1184. I would -- I would at this moment exclude for a second P1181, but for the others, are there objections against admission?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: There are, and it's a little difficult to formulate them because of the changes in exhibit numbers, but it is our understanding that the ERN ranges in -- in particular, I think it is annex 10.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Include the statements to which objection has been taken in the motion and upon which the Trial Chamber has --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. So that would be P1184 where there are objections. I take it you would further have to explore what is -- what is in there --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sorry to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: -- to be cumbersome about this. But given that none of us have a properly printed-out set of annexes according to the index that was only served at 10.00 this morning, may we have the opportunity to cross-refer the objections to the current list of MFI'd exhibits and then return to the Trial Chamber with a response in relation to that, so we don't inadvertently confuse as one document finds its way, so to speak, into a different exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, then you have some work to do overnight. Mr. Re, for you perhaps some work to do overnight is -- the Chamber noticed that at P1181 is a document which is composed of many other documents, altogether approximately - pardon - 145 pages, many of these documents already being exhibited -- well, many -- at least some. Could you try to find out which ones are and which ones are not so that we can get an updated list. The Chamber would then appreciate to hear as soon as possible from Defence counsel on objections. Then, is there any other procedural matter we'd have to raise at this moment? If not -- of course, I meant in relation to Witness 69. Witness 69, this concludes your testimony in this court. The Chamber would like to thank you very much for coming to The Hague and for answering all the questions that were put to you. I wish you a safe trip home again. We adjourn until tomorrow, quarter past 2.00 in the afternoon. Mr. Registrar, I take it in this same courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. It's confirmed by Mr. Registrar that it will be the same courtroom. We stand adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
